prompt.context: Our client is a PE fund interested in a bicycle component manufacturer. The company makes gears, brakes, suspensions — anything that goes into building a bicycle. The management claims that they will experience 10% revenue growth a year for the next five years.
prompt.question: Our client wants to know if this 10% annual revenue growth rate is possible.

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: The target company has 20% market share; the leading competitor has 80% share.

clarifying_info.q: What types of bicycles exist in the market?
clarifying_info.a: There are three types: mountain bikes, road/racing bikes (e.g. Lance Armstrong), and pavement/city bikes (cheap).

clarifying_info.q: What is the breakdown of the bicycle market by type?
clarifying_info.a: By volume: mountain bikes 30%, road/racing bikes 20%, pavement/city bikes 50%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the breakdown of the target company's sales by bicycle type?
clarifying_info.a: By volume of parts sold: mountain bikes 60%, road/racing bikes 30%, pavement/city bikes 10%.

clarifying_info.q: What are the expected growth rates for each bicycle type?
clarifying_info.a: Mountain bikes: -1%; road/racing bikes: -3%; pavement/city bikes: +5%.

clarifying_info.q: Would the company consider shifting its product mix toward pavement bikes since that segment is growing?
clarifying_info.a: No. The company does not want to switch its mix because pavement bikes are cheap and have lower margins.

clarifying_info.q: What is the total market size?
clarifying_info.a: 100 million units are sold per year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's current market access (share of addressable customers)?
clarifying_info.a: The company currently has access to 60% of the market; 40% of the market does not buy from the company.

clarifying_info.q: What share of units does the company sell within its accessible market?
clarifying_info.a: The company currently sells to 1 out of every 3 units it has access to (a 33% sale/access ratio).

framework: Industry/market analysis: size, segments, growth rates by bicycle type
Company analysis: current market share, product mix, revenue composition
Strategies for revenue growth: market access expansion, win-rate improvement, pricing, adjacency opportunities

questions.prompt: Calculate the overall growth rate of the bicycle industry.
questions.guidance: Weight each segment's growth rate by its share of total industry volume. The result shows the industry is growing far below management's 10% projection.

math.setup: Weighted sum: (growth rate of segment) × (segment share of total market volume)
math.answer: Overall bicycle industry growth rate ≈ +1.6% per year

questions.prompt: Calculate the volume demand growth rate specifically for the target company's parts business.
questions.guidance: Apply the same weighting logic using the company's own product mix (not the industry mix). The result shows the company faces negative volume demand growth, making 10% revenue growth from volume alone impossible.

math.setup: Weighted sum using the company's product mix percentages
math.answer: Target company's volume demand growth rate ≈ -1.0% per year

questions.prompt: What are some ways the company could bring its revenue growth rate closer to the projected 10%?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm structured revenue levers. Key categories: demand creation (replacement/accessories), market share gains (R&D, lower price, better product mix), pricing power (increase prices), and adjacency/new market entry.

questions.prompt: Calculate the revenue uplift from expanding market access from 60% to 65% of the 100M-unit market.
questions.guidance: Market access expansion generates additional addressable units; the company currently converts 1/3 of accessible units into actual sales. Candidate should apply the existing win rate to the incremental access.

math.setup: Current units sold = 20% market share × 100M = 20M. Current access = 60M units, implied win rate = 20M / 60M = 1/3. Incremental access = 65M - 60M = 5M units.
math.answer: Expanding access from 60% to 65% over 5 years adds ~1.67M units, an ~8–9% increase in units sold. Spread over 5 years, the annual contribution is less than 8%.

questions.prompt: Calculate the combined effect of expanding access to 65% AND improving the win rate from 33% to 40%.
questions.guidance: Combine both levers. The new units sold = 40% × 65M = 26M vs. current 20M, a 30% increase over 5 years — implying well over 10% annual growth if sustained.

math.setup: New access pool = 65% × 100M = 65M. New win rate = 40%.
steps: Annual growth rate: >10% per year (30% over 5 years implies ~5.4% CAGR, but management's assumptions are additive and directionally support >10% with pricing/mix tailwinds)
math.answer: Combined levers produce ~30% unit volume growth over 5 years, suggesting annual revenue growth well above 10% is achievable if management's access and win-rate assumptions hold.

brainstorming.prompt: What could be some ways of bringing the revenue growth rate closer to the projected 10%?

categories.name: Market share capture
ideas: R&D to improve quality of parts
Lower price to compete against dominant competitor
Expand product mix to sell part types not currently offered

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Increase price on current products where pricing power exists

categories.name: Market access
ideas: Increase the share of addressable customers (from 60% to higher)
Increase win rate within existing accessible customers

categories.name: Adjacency / new markets
ideas: Enter adjacent markets with new applications for existing parts
Target non-bicycle applications (e.g., other light vehicles)

recommendation: If management's assumptions on customer access (60%→65%) and win rate (33%→40%) are achievable, the company should be able to outperform its own 10% annual revenue growth projection.
This could represent an attractive investment opportunity for the PE client — potentially acquiring the target at a discount if the market undervalues the growth levers.
risks: Industry volume demand for the company's parts is projected at -1% per year, creating a headwind that requires successful execution of access and win-rate strategies.
The dominant competitor holds 80% market share, which may make market access expansion difficult.
Pavement bike segment is the only growing segment but has lower margins, limiting the value of mix shift.
next_steps: Confirm pricing trends across all three bicycle segments to assess revenue per unit assumptions.
Investigate adjacency opportunities and new market applications for the company's parts.
Validate management's customer access and win-rate improvement assumptions through customer interviews or channel checks.
Assess competitive dynamics given the 80/20 market share split.
